nonferrous-001.question: Which is the correct pairing of the thousands digit of the four-digit designation of wrought aluminum alloys with the main alloying element?
choices: 2000 series Zn, 5000 series Si, 6000 series Cu, 7000 series Mg
2000 series Cu, 5000 series Mg, 6000 series Mg and Si, 7000 series Zn
2000 series Mg, 5000 series Mn, 6000 series Cu and Mg, 7000 series Si
nonferrous-001.explanation: The thousands digit indicates the main alloying element: the 1000 series is pure aluminum (at least 99.00%), the 2000 series Cu, the 3000 series Mn, the 4000 series Si, the 5000 series Mg, the 6000 series Mg and Si, and the 7000 series Zn (most also contain Mg and Cu). 2000-series alloys such as 2024 are used in aircraft as duralumin; 5000-series alloys such as 5052 and 5083 are used in ships and containers for their corrosion resistance and weldability; 6000-series alloys such as 6061 and 6063 are used for extruded sections; and 7000-series alloys such as 7075, the strongest, are used in aircraft and sports equipment. The 2000, 6000 and 7000 series are heat-treatable alloys strengthened by precipitation hardening, while the 1000, 3000 and 5000 series are non-heat-treatable alloys strengthened by work hardening and solid-solution strengthening. The other pairings are mistakes that swap the elements between series.

nonferrous-002.question: In the ASTM designation system for magnesium alloys, what does “AZ91,” widely used for die casting, stand for?
choices: An alloy whose main additions are Al and Zn, with about 9 mass% Al and about 1 mass% Zn
An alloy whose main additions are Al and Zr, with about 9 mass% Al and about 0.1 mass% Zr
An alloy whose main additions are Zn and Al, with about 9 mass% Zn and about 1 mass% Al
nonferrous-002.explanation: In the ASTM system the two main alloying elements are given one letter each in decreasing order of content (A for Al, Z for Zn, M for Mn, K for Zr, E for rare earths, W for Y and so on), and the numbers that follow are their rounded mass percentages. AZ91 contains about 9% Al and about 1% Zn, and a final letter, as in AZ91D, distinguishes stages of improvement such as tighter control of impurities. The letter for Zr is K, so reading Z as Zr is wrong. The numbers follow the order of the letters, so reading Zn as 9% is also wrong. Al raises strength through solid-solution strengthening and the formation of Mg₁₇Al₁₂ during solidification and precipitation, and it improves fluidity and castability, but too much lowers ductility. AZ31 (about 3% Al and about 1% Zn) is commonly used for wrought products.

nonferrous-003.question: Among the temper designations of aluminum alloys, what does “H34,” used for alloys such as 5052, stand for?
choices: Solution heat-treated, cold-worked and artificially aged, with the hardness adjusted to 40% of the hardest state
Strain-hardened and then partially annealed, with the hardness brought back to three quarters of the hardest state
Strain-hardened and then heated at low temperature to stabilize the properties, with a hardness midway between O and the hardest state
nonferrous-003.explanation: H denotes strain-hardened material; the first digit indicates the treatment after working and the second the degree of hardness. H1x is strain-hardened only, H2x strain-hardened and then partially annealed, and H3x strain-hardened and then stabilized by low-temperature heating. A second digit of 8 is the hardest state, 4 is half-hard, midway between O (annealed) and 8, 2 is quarter-hard and 6 three-quarter-hard. 5000-series alloys with high Mg contents gradually soften and change their properties when kept at room temperature, so H3x tempers, given a low-temperature heating in advance to stop this, are used. Solution treatment and aging are treatments of the T tempers of heat-treatable alloys and are not applied to the non-heat-treatable 5052. Partial annealing is H2x, and a second digit of 4 means half-hard.

nonferrous-004.question: Consider why aluminum is used for overhead power lines by comparing the masses of conductors of the same length and the same electrical resistance. Taking the conductivities as 61% IACS for aluminum and 100% IACS for copper, and the densities as 2.70 g/cm³ for aluminum and 8.96 g/cm³ for copper, about how many times the mass of the copper conductor is the mass of the aluminum conductor?
choices: About 0.30 times
About 1.6 times
About 0.49 times
nonferrous-004.explanation: To keep the resistance R = ρL/A the same, aluminum, with 0.61 times the conductivity, needs 1/0.61 ≈ 1.64 times the cross-sectional area. Mass is proportional to cross-sectional area and density, so the ratio is 1.64 × 2.70/8.96 ≈ 0.49, about half that of copper. About 0.30 times compares only the densities and forgets the difference in conductivity, and about 1.6 times mistakes the ratio of areas for the ratio of masses. The wire becomes thicker, but because it is lighter the load on the towers falls and they can be spaced farther apart. For overhead lines, aluminum conductor steel-reinforced cable, with aluminum wires stranded around a steel core to add strength, is used. Where thickness is limited, as in wiring inside equipment, copper, with its higher conductivity per unit volume, has the advantage.

nonferrous-005.question: Sheet of alloys such as 2024 used for aircraft skins is often supplied as clad sheet (Alclad), with thin layers of pure aluminum or an Al-Zn alloy roll-bonded to both faces. Which is the main role of these layers?
choices: The surface layer is nobler and harder than the core, so even when scratched it acts as a protective film that stops the core from dissolving
The surface layer is more active (less noble) than the core, so where the core is exposed at scratches or cut edges, the layer dissolves first and protects the core electrochemically
The surface layer melts on heating and fills gaps at joints, preventing fatigue cracks from starting around rivet holes
nonferrous-005.explanation: Cu-containing 2000-series alloys are strong but prone to localized and intergranular corrosion around Cu-bearing precipitates, so their corrosion resistance is poor. Layers of pure aluminum or Al-1%Zn alloy a few percent of the sheet thickness are therefore roll-bonded to both faces. This cladding is more active than the core, so where the core is exposed at scratches or cut edges, the cladding dissolves first like a sacrificial anode and protects it. If the cladding were nobler, the exposed core would instead corrode faster through galvanic corrosion, so the option of a noble layer is wrong. Melting on heating to fill gaps is the role of the cladding on brazing sheet. Because the cladding is weak, the overall strength and fatigue strength of the sheet are slightly lower, and the sheet thickness is chosen with this in mind.

nonferrous-006.question: When an Al-Cu alloy is solution treated, quenched and aged, the precipitates change roughly in the sequence GP zones → θ'' → θ' → θ (Al₂Cu). Which statement about GP zones is correct?
choices: They are disk-shaped clusters of Cu atoms one to a few atomic layers thick on the {100} planes of the matrix, fully coherent with it and able to form even during aging at room temperature
They are narrow Cu-depleted zones along grain boundaries where no precipitates form, causing the regions near grain boundaries to be soft
They are coarse intragranular precipitates of the equilibrium θ (Al₂Cu) phase with incoherent interfaces with the matrix, appearing at the overaged stage
nonferrous-006.explanation: Cu atoms made supersaturated by quenching first gather on the {100} planes of the matrix to form disk-shaped GP zones one to a few atomic layers thick and a few nanometers across. They keep the crystal structure of the matrix and are fully coherent, and with their small interface energy the nucleation barrier is low, so with the help of excess vacancies retained by quenching they form even at room temperature and are responsible for the hardening of natural aging. As aging proceeds, the alloy passes through the coherent and semicoherent intermediate phases θ'' and θ' to the incoherent, coarse equilibrium phase θ and softens on overaging. The band near grain boundaries where Cu and vacancies are depleted and no precipitates form is the precipitate-free zone (PFZ), a different thing from GP zones. Coarse θ is not a GP zone but the equilibrium phase of the final stage of aging.

nonferrous-007.question: For thick plate and forgings of alloy 7075, the overaged T73 temper is sometimes chosen over T6, which gives the highest strength. Which is the main reason?
choices: In T73 the precipitates are finer and denser than in T6, so the strength rises considerably and the fatigue strength rises too
T73 skips artificial aging and is finished by natural aging alone, which lowers the cost of heat treatment and improves weldability
The strength is 10 to 15% lower than T6, but coarse, discontinuous grain-boundary precipitates raise resistance to stress corrosion cracking
nonferrous-007.explanation: The 7000 series, containing Zn, Mg and Cu, are the strongest aluminum alloys, but in the T6 condition, when tensile stress acts through the thickness of a thick part in a humid environment, stress corrosion cracking along grain boundaries readily occurs. T73 is an overaged temper in which aging is carried further than T6, at a higher temperature or for a longer time; the tensile and yield strengths are about 10 to 15% lower than T6, but the grain-boundary precipitates become coarse and discontinuous, so cracks along grain boundaries advance less easily. Overaging coarsens the precipitates, so the option in which they become finer and denser and raise the strength is backward. T7 indicates overaging; it does not skip aging, and finishing by natural aging alone corresponds to T4. Tempers such as T76 and T74, with other balances of strength and corrosion resistance, are also used.

nonferrous-008.question: Suppose that adding lithium to aluminum lowers the density by about 3% and raises Young's modulus by about 6% per mass% of Li. About how many times that of pure aluminum is the specific stiffness (Young's modulus/density) of an Al-Li alloy containing 2.0 mass% Li? Assume the changes are proportional to the amount added.
choices: About 1.06 times
About 1.19 times
About 1.12 times
nonferrous-008.explanation: At 2.0% Li, the density becomes 1 − 0.03 × 2.0 = 0.94 times and Young's modulus 1 + 0.06 × 2.0 = 1.12 times. The specific stiffness is their ratio, 1.12/0.94 ≈ 1.19 times, an improvement of about 19%. About 1.06 times subtracts the 6% fall in density from the 12% rise in modulus, and about 1.12 times compares only the change in modulus. Most alloying elements hardly change Young's modulus or density, so the specific stiffness of aluminum alloys is nearly constant, but Li is an exceptional element: its atoms are very light, and it forms the ordered phase Al₃Li (δ') that also raises stiffness. 2.0 mass% Li corresponds to about 7 at%. Al-Cu-Li alloys, improved to overcome problems of anisotropy and toughness, are used in aircraft structures.

nonferrous-009.question: Tough-pitch copper (copper containing about 0.02 to 0.05% oxygen, mostly dispersed as Cu₂O) can become brittle when it is heated in a reducing atmosphere containing hydrogen or is gas welded or brazed. Which gives the correct cause and remedy?
choices: Hydrogen that enters reacts with Cu₂O to form steam, which creates high-pressure cavities and cracks at grain boundaries, so oxygen-free copper or phosphorus-deoxidized copper is used
Hydrogen that enters reacts with copper to form hard hydrides at grain boundaries, so a high-temperature anneal after heating is used to decompose the hydrides
Cu₂O melts on heating and forms a liquid film at grain boundaries, so copper with even more oxygen, in which the Cu₂O has been made large and round, is used
nonferrous-009.explanation: Hydrogen that diffuses into copper reacts with Cu₂O at grain boundaries and elsewhere as Cu₂O + H₂ → 2Cu + H₂O, and because water molecules cannot diffuse through copper, they create high-pressure cavities at grain boundaries that lead to cracking. This is called hydrogen embrittlement of copper (hydrogen sickness). The remedy is to use oxygen-free copper, which contains almost no oxygen, or phosphorus-deoxidized copper. Residual phosphorus lowers the conductivity of phosphorus-deoxidized copper, so oxygen-free copper is used where high conductivity is needed. Copper does not form stable hydrides, so the option blaming hydrides is wrong. Nor is the embrittlement caused by melting of Cu₂O; adding more oxygen only increases the source of steam.

nonferrous-010.question: Among copper alloys for springs and connectors, which is the correct pairing of the strengthening mechanisms of phosphor bronze and beryllium copper?
choices: Phosphor bronze is strengthened by precipitation hardening with phosphides, and beryllium copper by solid-solution strengthening with Be and work hardening by cold work
Both are strengthened by martensitic transformation on quenching and then tempered to adjust toughness and spring properties
Phosphor bronze is strengthened by solid-solution strengthening with Sn and work hardening by cold work, and beryllium copper by precipitation hardening through solution treatment and aging
nonferrous-010.explanation: Phosphor bronze is copper with a few percent of Sn, deoxidized with a little P; its spring strength comes from solid-solution strengthening by Sn and work hardening by cold rolling, and it is not hardened by heat treatment. Beryllium copper contains about 2% Be; when solution treated at about 800 °C, quenched and aged at about 300 °C, fine precipitates form and its tensile strength exceeds 1 GPa, the highest among copper alloys. Its conductivity is also fairly good, and it is used for spark-resistant tools as well, but Be dust and fumes are harmful, so precautions against inhaling them are needed in processing. The option citing phosphide precipitation and Be in solid solution mixes up the mechanisms of the two alloys. Neither alloy is strengthened by martensitic transformation on quenching as steel is.

nonferrous-011.question: The corrosion resistance of magnesium alloys depends strongly on the amounts of the impurities Fe, Ni and Cu, and in high-purity alloys such as AZ91D the upper limits for Fe and Ni are set very low, at about 0.005% or less. Which is the correct reason?
choices: These elements dissolve in Mg and make the matrix potential more active, so the surface oxide film grows too thick and cracks easily
These elements appear as particles nobler than Mg and form local cells with the surrounding Mg, accelerating its dissolution
These elements promote oxidation of the melt and make it more flammable, so oxides entrapped during casting increase the sites where corrosion starts
nonferrous-011.explanation: Mg is one of the most active of the practical metals. Even small amounts of Fe, Ni and Cu hardly dissolve in Mg and appear as particles of metals or intermetallic compounds with a noble potential. Local cells form in which these particles are cathodes and the surrounding Mg is the anode, and in salt water the corrosion rate becomes orders of magnitude larger. In high-purity alloys, therefore, Fe and Ni are held to very small amounts and Cu to about 0.03% or less, and Mn is added to take Fe into Al-Mn-Fe compounds and reduce its harm. The option in which the elements dissolve and thicken the film and the option explaining it by the flammability of the melt both miss this local-cell mechanism. For the same reason, insulation is needed when Mg parts are in contact with steel bolts.

nonferrous-012.question: A flat panel whose thickness is chosen to give a fixed bending stiffness is changed from an aluminum alloy (Young's modulus 70 GPa, density 2.70 g/cm³) to a magnesium alloy (Young's modulus 45 GPa, density 1.74 g/cm³). If the area of the panel is the same and the bending stiffness is proportional to E × (thickness)³, about how many times the mass of the aluminum alloy panel is the mass of the magnesium alloy panel?
choices: About 0.75 times
About 0.64 times
About 1.0 times
nonferrous-012.explanation: To keep the bending stiffness E·t³ the same, the thickness must be increased by (70/45)^(1/3) ≈ 1.16 times. Mass is proportional to thickness and density, so the ratio is 1.16 × 1.74/2.70 ≈ 0.75, about 25% lighter. About 0.64 times compares only the densities without changing the thickness, which leaves the stiffness too low. About 1.0 times assumes the stiffness is proportional to Young's modulus and increases the thickness by 70/45; that is how members governed by tensile stiffness compare. E/ρ is about 25 GPa/(g/cm³) for Mg, Al, Ti and steel alike, so they give no weight saving in tensile stiffness, but in panels whose thickness can be increased, the lower-density metals have the advantage. This is one reason magnesium alloy die castings are used for thin housings and automotive interior parts.

nonferrous-013.question: In α+β titanium alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V, cooling from above the β transus gives a lamellar structure of colonies of plate-like α, while working below the β transus and annealing gives a structure containing equiaxed α. Which statement about the difference in properties between these two structures is correct?
choices: The lamellar structure has greater ductility and resistance to fatigue crack initiation, and the equiaxed structure has greater fracture toughness and resistance to fatigue crack growth
The equiaxed structure has greater ductility and resistance to fatigue crack initiation, and the lamellar structure has greater fracture toughness and resistance to fatigue crack growth
The two differ only in the distribution of grain orientations, and their tensile strength, ductility, fracture toughness and fatigue properties are almost the same
nonferrous-013.explanation: Equiaxed structures (worked below the β transus and recrystallized, or bimodal structures mixing equiaxed α with lamellar regions) have short slip lengths and distribute deformation evenly, so they have greater ductility and resist the initiation of fatigue cracks. In the lamellar structure cooled from above the β transus, on the other hand, cracks follow a tortuous path along the colonies of plate-like α, so the crack path is longer, the fracture toughness is higher and long cracks grow more slowly. The lamellar structure is also better in creep strength at high temperature. The option that swaps the two sets of properties is wrong, and because the shape of the microstructure strongly affects mechanical properties, the option saying they are almost the same is also wrong. Microstructures are tailored to the properties each part needs through the working temperature and cooling rate.

nonferrous-014.question: In designing α and α+β titanium alloys, the effect of α-stabilizing elements is summarized by the aluminum equivalent [Al]eq = [Al] + [Sn]/3 + [Zr]/6 + 10[O] (mass%), with a guideline that it should not exceed about 9. For a Ti-6Al-2Sn-4Zr-2Mo alloy containing 0.10 mass% oxygen, which is closest to [Al]eq?
choices: About 8.3
About 7.4
About 13
nonferrous-014.explanation: [Al]eq = 6 + 2/3 + 4/6 + 10 × 0.10 = 6 + 0.67 + 0.67 + 1.0 ≈ 8.3, below the guideline of 9. About 7.4 forgets to multiply oxygen by its coefficient of 10, and about 13 adds Sn and Zr without dividing by their coefficients. If the aluminum equivalent is too high, the ordered phase α₂ (Ti₃Al) precipitates in the α phase, lowering ductility and resistance to stress corrosion cracking. As the fact that a mere 0.1% oxygen counts as much as 1% aluminum shows, interstitial oxygen strongly stabilizes the α phase and raises strength, so the oxygen content is an important control item that distinguishes grades of an alloy. Mo is a β-stabilizing element and does not enter this expression.

nonferrous-015.question: The Ni-based alloy 718 (a Ni-Cr-Fe alloy containing about 5% Nb) is widely used for jet engine disks and similar parts. Which statement about its strengthening and characteristics is correct?
choices: It is strengthened mainly by L1₂ γ' (Ni₃Al), which precipitates quickly so it is prone to strain-age cracking in post-weld heat treatment, but it keeps its strength above 1000 °C
It is a solid-solution-strengthened alloy without precipitates, low in strength but excellent in corrosion resistance, and used mainly for chemical plant piping
It is strengthened mainly by body-centered tetragonal γ'' (Ni₃Nb), which precipitates slowly so it resists post-weld cracking, but in long use above about 650 °C it turns to δ phase and softens
nonferrous-015.explanation: In alloy 718, Nb precipitates coherently with the matrix as the body-centered tetragonal ordered phase γ'' (Ni₃Nb), which provides strengthening together with a small amount of γ'. Because γ'' precipitates more slowly than γ', strain-age cracking, which occurs when shrinkage from precipitation combines with residual stress during the aging heat after welding, is unlikely, so the alloy suits parts assembled by welding. γ'', however, is metastable, and with long use above about 650 °C it coarsens and transforms to the stable orthorhombic δ phase (Ni₃Nb), so the strength falls. The alloys used above 1000 °C are those rich in γ', such as single-crystal blade alloys. Alloy 718 is a high-strength precipitation-strengthened alloy, so the option calling it solid-solution strengthened is also wrong.
